name: vampire
why: A high-performance first-order theorem prover; a real logic engine worth poking at, though its appeal is niche and academic.

brief.what_it_is: Vampire is an automated theorem prover, a program that tries to prove logical statements. Its main focus is first-order logic, and it can also disprove non-theorems, build finite models, and reason in combinations of theories such as arithmetic, arrays, and datatypes. Input is a problem file in TPTP format (or SMT-LIB, since it can act as an SMT solver), and output is a verdict plus, on request, a detailed proof or a finite model. Its homepage says it is increasingly able to handle higher-order logic.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames automatic theorem proving as useful for software and hardware verification, knowledge representation, the Semantic Web, algebra, and mathematics. It presents Vampire as a way to turn the superposition calculus, which it calls one of the most advanced and elegant theories in computer science, into practically valuable tools. Development began in 1994.
brief.how_it_works: The README gives no internal mechanism beyond the portfolio idea: the default mode runs with a 60 second time limit, while the casc portfolio mode tries many different strategies, which the README says often performs better. The homepage names the superposition calculus as the core theory and says the portfolio mode can run in multicore mode. It also says Vampire supports inductive reasoning over algebraic data types (finite term algebras).

commands_seen.context: Basic usage: runs Vampire in its default mode on a TPTP problem file, with a 60 second time limit.
Runs portfolio mode, which tries many strategies; the README says this often beats the default mode.

brief.install_notes: The README says pre-built binaries are on the GitHub releases page and that one probably exists for your platform. If not, you build from source, which the README calls not too onerous; the build steps are on the wiki page 'Source Build for Users'. The project links to MiniSat, CaDiCaL, GMP (mini-gmp part), and VIRAS, and Z3 is optional. Input problems are expected in TPTP format. No accounts or runtimes are mentioned.
brief.standout: It is a serious research-grade prover with competition awards at CASC and SMT-COMP, and it is unusual in that one binary covers first-order proving, model finding, SMT-LIB input, and inductive reasoning over datatypes. Its portfolio mode gives one-command access to many strategies at once.
brief.status: Appears maintained, though I could not confirm dates. The GitHub page shows an active CI badge and the homepage describes ongoing development, but I saw no release date or last-commit date in the pages I read, so this is inferred rather than confirmed.
brief.caveats: The README does not state platform support beyond saying pre-built binaries may exist, so a source build may be needed. The licence is BSD-3-Clause per the badge, but the README points to a LICENCE file for details. Z3 is optional and some bundled dependencies carry their own licences. The homepage's appeal is niche and academic, and the tool expects TPTP-formatted input, so it is not a general-purpose tool for casual users.

judge.reason: Vampire makes the elegant superposition calculus tangible, proving or finding models for logical statements in a research-grade tool most developers rarely encounter.

entry.title: Vampire
entry.tldr: A research-grade automated theorem prover: give it a logical problem in TPTP format and it tries to prove it, refute it, or build a model.
entry.deeper_look:
Vampire is an automated theorem prover, a program that tries to prove logical statements without a human steering it. Its main focus is first-order logic. It can also disprove non-theorems, build finite models, and reason with theories such as arithmetic, arrays, and datatypes. It reads problems in TPTP format, or SMT-LIB since it can act as an SMT solver, and prints a verdict. On request it also prints a detailed proof or a finite model.

The project's homepage says development began in 1994. It describes the superposition calculus as "one of the most advanced and elegant theories in computer science", and presents Vampire as a way to turn that theory into practical tools. The uses it lists are software and hardware verification, knowledge representation, the Semantic Web, algebra, and mathematics. It also supports inductive reasoning over algebraic data types, and the homepage says higher-order logic is increasingly handled.

The door into something larger is the idea of a portfolio. No single proof strategy works on every problem, so the `casc` mode tries many strategies, and the README says it often beats the default. The default mode runs with a 60 second time limit. Reading the proof output, then switching modes to see how the verdict changes, is a hands-on way into automated reasoning.
entry.install:
brew install vampire
# Pre-built binaries are also on the GitHub releases page. Problems must be written in TPTP format (see tptp.org).

try_this.what_happens: Runs Vampire in its default mode on a TPTP problem file, with a 60 second time limit.
Runs portfolio mode, which tries many strategies and often does better than the default.
Uses a portfolio variant tuned for satisfiable problems, handy when you suspect the problem has a model.

entry.whats_unique: One binary covers first-order proving, model finding, SMT-LIB input, and induction over datatypes. It comes from a prover with competition awards at CASC and SMT-COMP, and portfolio mode gives one-command access to many strategies.
entry.caveats: It expects TPTP-formatted input and its appeal is niche and academic, so you will need to write or fetch a problem file before anything interesting happens.
